newsitem.title: USA: Selecting the right IRA will be big 1998 decision.
newsitem.headline: Selecting the right IRA will be big 1998 decision.

text.p: There are many little gifts in the tax bill that President Clinton signed this week, but most don't require heavy duty decision-making: For example, you either have the kids and get the credit, or you don't.

That's not the case with the variety of Individual Retirement Accounts that become fully available next year. Taxpayers will have more IRA choices than before and will be responsible for figuring out which is best for them.
First, here's a description of the new options that become available on Jan. 1.

Anyone who is not covered by a pension plan at work (even if their spouse is) may have a traditional, tax deferred IRA. Annual contributions of up to $2,000 in these IRAs are tax deductible when you deposit the money; every penny withdrawn from one of these accounts is taxed as income when it's withdrawn.

Money withdrawn before you are 59-1/2 is also subject to a 10 percent penalty, unless it is used for higher education or a first-time home purchase. Even if you're covered by a plan at work, you can have one of these fully deductible IRAs if you're part of a couple earning less than $60,000 a year or earn less than $40,000 a year as an individual taxpayer.

Any individuals earning less than $110,000 or couples earning less than $160,000 may open a new "Roth IRA" even if they already have a plan at work. These plans are fed with after-tax contributions of as much as $2,000, but all of the money taken out of these accounts for a first-time home purchase, disability or after you've turned 59-1/2 is tax free, as long as the account has existed for five years.

The new legislation also allows people who own existing IRAs to roll over their IRAs into a new Roth IRA by paying tax on the tax-deferred amounts in the account. If you decide to make that transfer in 1998, you get four years to spread out the taxes.

There's no excuse now for not taking advantage of every IRA deal you can. The current bill eliminates the penalty tax that used to be levied on IRAs that got too big. Now, there's no such thing as an IRA with too much money in it.

What should you do next year? That depends on many specifics of your situation, but here's a rough guide. First, feed your 401(k) plan as much as you're allowed. Your contributions to this plan may be matched by your employer; they come out of your paycheck in a pretty painless manner, and they don't hurt your ability to establish an IRA if you're otherwise entitled.

Then, decide which IRA is best for you. If you are young, have a low tax rate and believe you can let the money compound for years and years, establish a Roth IRA, suggests Joan Vines of Grant Thornton, an accounting firm. She notes that Roth IRAs do not require you to start taking money out at age 70-1/2, as do traditional IRAs. So if you intend to have other money to live on and want your retirement kitty to compound and compound, the Roth IRAs are a good choice.

If you are nearing retirement, expect your post-retirement tax rate to be significantly lower than it is now, or need every penny of tax write-off in 1998 so you can afford a $2,000 contribution, go for the traditional IRA.

Should you transfer existing IRAs into new tax-free Roth specials? Yes, if you fit that young, low-tax-rate profile of a Roth IRA winner and can keep the extra tax liability from destroying your family finances in the short term.

What if you fall in the middle of these profiles? You have until April 15, 1999 to decide what you're going to elect for tax year 1998. Spend some of that time -- and some of that cash -- finding a qualified accountant who can crunch the numbers and tell you which way is best.
